# Brief: build the real AI Peer (2026-11-04)

Written once, on 2026-11-04. Manish's request at the start of the build, verbatim
(voice dictation, so a few product names are likely transcription errors; see
the notes at the end). For the hand-off copy (7 Nov), a few spans about the old test
company or his own accounts were cut; each cut is marked "[…]" or "[test-company
detail removed]". The living decisions go in the design doc's §0.

## Manish's words

I had an idea related to a hackathon, which I'm going to take up in Airbnb. So Airbnb has a year-end hackathon around November, 16th November to 20th November. There I'm planning to implement this idea. And there is a repo […], if I'm not wrong. You can check that. You can download that repo to understand at a high level what this idea is all about. And I also tried to create a demo video to showcase it. You can also check that demo video. But at a high level, the idea is about creating an AI peer, by which you are giving AI the power that it needs to be proactive and to discover things on its own, not just respond. Similar to how we see these new products in the market, like GroqBot or Claude Duet or ChatGPT Dot, things like that. So the name can still be changed, but that was the high-level idea. So one thing I was thinking was: let's see how this is going to look. So in this session, I'm just going to create all my thoughts, whatever thoughts I have right now, with you, and then I will need you to process all these thoughts, do your own research, come up with your own ideas, and with that, we try to come to a shared understanding of what exactly we need to develop, and how we should approach this, and how this is going to evolve. But I'm very sure that this is going to span across multiple weeks and multiple sessions. So we need to set up ways of working so that we can keep on going without losing any key information and make progress, and have the project ready in time before the hackathon. So now let's talk about it. Let's talk about how anyone would set this up.

So in the setup, I would like it to be a one-click setup. You come to your profile and the user clicks on that, like "Create my AI peer" or something like that. And then, because we are triggering it from their profile, they know for whom we are creating this AI peer, for which employee, and what is their team, what is their role, what are the services and systems that they own, where is the code for those services and systems. So with that, it should be able to understand each and every piece of information that is relevant for a given employee. And again, here the AI peer we are creating is at an individual employee level. So if I'm creating an AI peer for me, my idea is that it knows everything that I know, so it can fill the gap wherever my presence is needed, but I can't be available. That AI peer can fill that gap. And similarly, wherever something is going on in the company, something important for me, but I'm not aware of that, it can bring that information to me as well. So both ways it is filling the gap between the employee and the company. So now, coming back to the setup, I'm thinking it should be that one-click setup where it understands the team, the services, the systems, tools, the code base, everything. And in Airbnb, we have the one.airbnb.com portal, where we have all this context about a given employee. So maybe we can integrate with that to get information about a given employee. Then, like we talked about, for code, it can use GitHub or Sourcegraph to understand whatever code is committed already to GitHub. But even locally: what if there is a lot of work that the employee has set up on their local Mac? So it should understand that as well. Because it's very important to understand their local setup or local nodes, everything. And in local, we use a coding agent, which is named AirChat. Internally, it uses Codex or Claude Code. So maybe we can add that as a plugin of AirChat as well, so that it can process all the local nodes and local code and more context about that employee. And then more understanding of the context can be done from Google Docs or Slack or any other company resources. So with all of that, it will be able to build a knowledge store about you and your team and your tools and services. So it will build this knowledge store in an efficient manner so that whenever it needs to fetch something, it can fetch that information. And also it knows how to keep it up to date.

Next, it has to be proactive. Like we talked about. So it will monitor the configured systems, and it will act whenever it identifies a change based on the role it is playing. So like I talked about, it is going to be a one-click setup where ideally you would give it access to everything, and you would want it to act on everything. But you can also customize it. So let's say you only want it to access your services' code base, and whenever anything relevant to that code base is happening anywhere else, like on Slack or maybe in Google Docs, it can keep an eye there, and it does its responsibility and role, which again, you can customize. You can say that, "Only focus whenever there is an issue," or something like that. So while it is a one-click setup, we would want to provide all those customizations as well. And over time, it should be able to update itself, so that it is updating its own configuration based on what the user wants now versus whenever they want to update the setting.

And I can give you some examples on what are the things that can be happening. So let's say I own service A, and I'm working on a project, P1. Now, there is some Slack thread going on, which is asking about an update on this P1 project for a given feature, or related to any dependency or something. But I'm not aware of that. Even they are not aware who is the right POC from my team for this project. But because this AI peer has full context, it can get that information. And so it will go to that Slack thread, and it will reply on my behalf if I'm not available. If I'm available, then it can just let me know that, "Hey, this discussion is going on. Do you want to go and provide an update?" or something like that. Similarly, a dependent system might have changed. That can break our system. So it will let me know about that. Let's say there is a late night Zoom meeting that I should attend, but I'm not able to because it's very late night for me. So this AI peer can attend on my behalf and join that call and provide an update on my behalf. And when I wake up, it can bring me up to speed on what happened in that Zoom call, and if there are any takeaways for me. Or let's say there is an important event or initiative happening in the company that aligns with my interest, but I'm not aware of that, so it will let me know of that. So it means we need to integrate with multiple surfaces like Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Zoom, Google Docs, everywhere, so that it can know everything, monitor everything, and act anywhere. So this is the setup-related thing and monitor-and-act-related stuff that we talked about.

Now, what about the implementation approach? So if you think about the implementation approach, then we are building this for Airbnb, and there will definitely be Airbnb-specific integration that we will have to do eventually. But those integrations are sometimes tricky. We might or might not be able to make all those integrations work as well within the time limit that we have for the hackathon. So my idea is that initially I'm going to build a generic system, where I will try to have generic integration or a specific integration, which is my own, let's say […]. So we will use that to build a generic implemented system, which I will try to later fit into Airbnb-specific integration. So think about it. The system is ready. It is integrated with some X system. That X system is my own personal system. So I was saying that just by changing the integration from my personal X system to the Airbnb system, the solution should then work for Airbnb. That's why when we are designing the solution, when we are implementing the solution, we have to keep this point in mind. And we can decouple the integration part from the main implementation and also document that this is how the system works. This is how we can integrate it with one specific system, whether it is Airbnb or any other company. So that later on, when we need to make it Airbnb-specific, we just need to make those integrations work. The rest of the application still works seamlessly.

And again, here we have to follow most of our ways of working like we do for the [test-company detail removed] repo. Like how we have the repo as the source of truth, where we don't have to depend on any given coding agent's previous chat sessions or anything. Whatever is there, it's part of the repo. And, like I mentioned, we will test it with the small test company setup, where I will provide you […]. But then we will change the integration so that it can work for Airbnb or even any other company if we need that in future. We have to think about all those ways of working that I was talking about, that we use for [test-company detail removed]. Like how we have the repo as the source of truth, and how a big initiative is controlled through controller sessions that control other individual worker sessions, and they provide handoff around forty-five to fifty percent of context. And we have to remember that this is a hackathon, so our main idea is to make it work, and not go off track in unimportant things like code quality, unit tests, et cetera. So we can just try to move fast and try to get to a working implementation as soon as possible, and we can always verify if it is working or not by manually testing it. Let's say we want to test it in the browser, we can do that. So we build something, we test it manually by running it in the browser or running through the terminal or whatever is the applicable way. We can do that, but try to move fast and not go off track. We have to remember that this is a hackathon project where code quality, safety issues, they don't matter as much. It's just like a POC that we need to finish in time for the hackathon. So that's the idea. But other than that, we should try to follow all our ways of working that we generally follow.

And for the AI part, I'm thinking what to use, but maybe we can just use my Claude Code subscription or Codex subscription when we actually want to run it. So I'm thinking maybe a skill that is constantly running: I can trigger that skill inside Claude Code, or I can trigger this skill inside Codex, which is something like a configurable thing. Because in Airbnb also, I mentioned that the harness that we use is AirChat, but internally, AirChat uses Claude Code or Codex. So this same setup should ideally work there as well if we build it for Claude Code and Codex. And in Airbnb, we also have an AirChat remote. So later on, not an urgent requirement, but later on we can see if they have an AirChat remote setup where they can provide us a twenty-four hours running machine with AirChat setup. So there I can keep it running. Then it will not have a dependency on my system to be up and running. But that we will evaluate later on.

And other ways of working we also need to follow, like how we have all the documents inside the repo, like the requirement document, learning document, goal document, tracker, any discussions, so that we build on our own learnings, and we have all the context that is important for us stored inside the repo in a compact manner, without losing any key information that is important for us to make progress. And it is also structured in a manner such that whenever something is needed, that context can be loaded on demand, without filling the full context window every time, for any need, for any session. We don't want that to happen. Rather, it should be structured, and a given piece of information can be fetched as and when it is needed. So I think that's how we need to think about how we want to build our internal memory store inside the repo, how it will be structured, folder structure, et cetera. So these are the ways of working that I had in mind.

And these are my initial thoughts. So I know this is a lot of information that I provided to you, but all of this is important information and the requirements that I could think of right now. But I would want you to be creative yourself, think outside the box, try to think about what exactly I am asking for, what exactly is needed, what else is there that I might be missing. Do your own research and come up with all those findings and analysis, and then process my requirements as well. And then let's start doing an interview, like how we generally do, where you ask me any question, any clarification, any assumption that you are making, so that once we are done with the interview, we are a hundred percent aligned on exactly what solution we are looking for and what approach we should take. So all of that should be very, very clear to us. So let's do that interview once you are ready, where you ask me one question at a time and explain that question to me in an easy-to-understand manner, in simplified language, and then also give me options to choose from with your recommendation, so that it's convenient for me to respond. And in case I want to provide my own response, that option should also be given by you. These are all the requirements from my side, and this is the hackathon project. Please process everything, and let's go.
